cards.title: Pytania wielokrotnego wyboru do tekstu
cards.body:
Najpierw przeczytaj pytanie, potem tekst. Dla każdej opcji sprawdź, czy tekst ją **potwierdza**, **zaprzecza** jej, czy o niej **milczy**; błędne opcje często zawierają prawdziwe słowa z tekstu użyte w złym kontekście.
Poprawna odpowiedź jest zwykle parafrazą zdania z tekstu, a nie jego kopią.

cards.title: Który akapit zawiera informację?
cards.body:
Najpierw **zrób mapę tekstu**: obok każdego akapitu zapisz w kilku słowach, o czym jest (pierwszy akapit często wprowadza temat, ostatni podsumowuje).
W pytaniach szukaj słów kluczowych (economic, trade-offs, remote areas) i ich synonimów. Akapit może być odpowiedzią na kilka pytań.
cards.tip: Pytanie bywa ogólniejsze niż akapit: dopasuj główną myśl, nie pojedyncze słowo.

cards.title: Czas w arkuszu wojewódzkim
cards.body:
Arkusz wojewódzki trwa **120 minut** i ma **100 punktów**.
Zadania czytania zajmują najwięcej czasu, ale mają stosunkowo mało punktów na minutę – zacznij od zadań językowych, które możesz zrobić szybko (idiomy, wybór A–D), potem wróć do tekstów. Zostaw 10 minut na przegląd.

flash.back: od mapy tekstu: krótkie hasło przy każdym akapicie

flash.front: Opcja A–D zawiera słowa z tekstu, ale w złym kontekście. Co to znaczy?
flash.back: To typowa opcja błędna – sprawdź, czy tekst naprawdę to potwierdza.

flash.front: Ile trwa arkusz wojewódzki i ile ma punktów?

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj uważnie tekst, a następnie odpowiedz na pytania, wybierając prawidłową odpowiedź A, B, C lub D. Za każdą poprawną odpowiedź otrzymasz 1 punkt.
groups.text:
The quiet revolution in public libraries

For years, predictions about the future of public libraries were gloomy. If books could be bought online in seconds and read on a tablet, many experts asked, who would need a building full of paper? Yet in several countries the number of library visitors has risen, and the reason is simple: libraries have stopped trying to be warehouses of books and have become meeting places.

A typical modern library offers far more than shelves. There are rooms where students can work in silence, studios where teenagers record podcasts, and workshops with 3D printers that anyone can use after a short introduction. Many libraries also run language cafés for newcomers to the country, who practise the local language with volunteers over a cup of tea. For people without a computer at home, a library may be the only place where they can apply for a job or fill in official forms online.

The change has not been easy. Budgets have been cut in many towns, and some councils have chosen to close small branches instead of investing in new services. Critics argue that a library without enough books is no longer a library at all. Librarians reply that their collections have not disappeared but have grown to include e-books, audiobooks and digital magazines, which can be borrowed without leaving home.

One example of a successful transformation is a library in a converted factory in a northern town. Opened five years ago, it attracts families at the weekend and pensioners on weekday mornings, when a team of volunteers teaches them how to use smartphones. The director says that the key was to ask the residents what they needed before planning anything. 'We did not guess,' she explains. 'We asked, and then we listened.'

Whether libraries can survive in the long term will depend on money, but also on imagination. The most successful ones seem to understand that a library's real value is not measured by the number of books it owns, but by the number of people who walk through its doors and leave a little better informed than they arrived.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj uważnie tekst, a następnie wskaż numer akapitu (1–6), w którym znajduje się podana informacja. Ten sam akapit może być odpowiedzią na więcej niż jedno pytanie. Za każdą poprawną odpowiedź otrzymasz 1 punkt.
groups.text:
Paragraph 1: The five-day working week, with a free Saturday and Sunday, is so familiar that it is easy to forget how recent it is. It became widespread during the twentieth century, after employers noticed that tired workers made more mistakes. Today, a growing number of companies are asking whether it is time for another change: a working week of four days.

Paragraph 2: The idea has been tested in several trials. In one trial involving thirty small firms, employees kept their full salaries but worked thirty-two hours instead of forty. After six months, almost every company decided to continue the arrangement, and several reported that fewer people had left their jobs.

Paragraph 3: Employees themselves describe the change in simple terms. They say they sleep longer, spend more time with their families and can finally find time for hobbies or medical appointments. Many report feeling less stressed on Monday mornings, and managers noticed that sick leave decreased.

Paragraph 4: Not everyone is convinced, however. Economists point out that the trials were small and that the firms that volunteered were probably the ones most likely to succeed. They warn that results might be different in companies where the pace of work is difficult to speed up, and that employees may simply work harder for four days and feel exhausted.

Paragraph 5: There are also practical problems. A hospital cannot close on Fridays, and a shop that is open seven days a week needs enough staff to cover every shift. Some organisations have solved this by dividing staff into groups with different days off, but this makes planning more complicated and can increase costs.

Paragraph 6: Whatever the final verdict, the discussion has already changed attitudes. Employers have begun to measure success by results rather than by hours spent in the office, and workers are more confident when they ask for flexible conditions. The four-day week may not suit every business, but it has shown that old habits can be questioned.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj uważnie tekst, a następnie odpowiedz na pytania, wybierając prawidłową odpowiedź A, B, C lub D.
groups.text:
When the council of a small mountain village announced that it would switch off the public Wi-Fi in the main square for the whole of August, many residents expected protests. Instead, the response surprised everyone. 'Within a week the square was full of people,' recalls café owner Hanna Voss. 'People who had not spoken for years were sitting at the same tables.'

The idea came from a teacher who noticed that teenagers spent their breaks staring at screens instead of playing outside. She suggested a month-long experiment, which the council agreed to on the condition that the village shops would stay connected to the internet so that nobody was cut off from essential services.

By the end of August, the results were mixed. Many parents were delighted, saying that their children had rediscovered football and cycling. Some young people, however, complained that the village had treated them like children, and one group of students organised a quiet protest by meeting in a car park outside the village, where the signal of a neighbouring town was strong.

Researchers from a nearby university, who followed the experiment, caution against drawing broad conclusions. They point out that a single month is too short to measure lasting changes and that August is a holiday period, when people behave differently anyway. Nevertheless, the village plans to repeat the project next summer, this time with a longer programme of events in the square, so that nobody feels there is nothing to do.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj uważnie tekst, a następnie wskaż numer akapitu (1–6), w którym znajduje się podana informacja. Ten sam akapit może być odpowiedzią na więcej niż jedno pytanie.
groups.text:
Paragraph 1: Walk through almost any large city and you will notice a pattern: old buildings disappear and glass-and-steel towers take their place. Many city authorities prefer modern construction, arguing that it is more efficient and attracts investors.

Paragraph 2: Supporters of preservation answer with economic arguments. Renovating an old building is often cheaper than constructing a new one of the same size, and historic districts bring in large amounts of money from tourists who come to admire them.

Paragraph 3: There is also an environmental argument. Demolition produces huge quantities of waste, and the materials and energy used to build the original structure are lost for ever. Architects call this hidden cost 'embodied energy'.

Paragraph 4: Old buildings also give a place its character. Residents often say that familiar streets and houses make them feel connected to their neighbourhood and to the people who lived there before them. When these buildings vanish, something intangible vanishes too.

Paragraph 5: Preservation is not without problems. Old houses can be cold, difficult to heat and hard to adapt for people with disabilities. Strict rules about what owners are allowed to change may also discourage them from investing in repairs.

Paragraph 6: A popular compromise is to give old buildings a new function. Railway stations have become museums, factories are now apartments and a former market hall houses a library. In such cases, the walls remain and the city gains a useful space.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj tekst, z którego usunięto 8 zdań. Dla każdej luki wybierz literę (A–I) oznaczającą brakujące zdanie tak, aby otrzymać spójny i logiczny tekst. Uwaga: 1 zdanie zostało podane dodatkowo i nie pasuje do żadnej luki.
groups.text:
From market stall to restaurant: Maya's story

Maya Torres was fifteen when she started helping her uncle at his vegetable stall in a busy city market. (1)___ She enjoyed talking to customers, but what she loved most was the moment when she took home the ugly tomatoes and bent carrots that nobody wanted to buy.

In the evenings she turned the unwanted vegetables into soups and stews for her neighbours. (2)___ Soon people were knocking on her door to ask if there was any soup left.

A local food blogger visited the stall one Saturday. (3)___ The article he wrote was short, but it brought hundreds of new visitors to the market the following week.

Success, however, came with problems. (4)___ Maya could not keep up with the demand, and she had never learned how to run a business.

Her uncle suggested asking a restaurant owner for advice. (5)___ Instead of giving her a long lecture, he offered her a job washing dishes and watching the cooks.

She learned more in six months than in all her previous years. (6)___ By the end of the year, she knew how to plan menus, order food and manage a small team.

When the restaurant owner decided to retire, he made her an unexpected offer. (7)___ Maya hesitated for a week and then accepted.

Today the small restaurant is fully booked every evening. (8)___ Maya says that the ugly carrots still have a special place on her menu.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)
bank: The man she chose turned out to be much kinder than she had feared.
Many young people dream of becoming chefs after watching cooking programmes on television.
Word about her cooking spread quickly around the block.
He proposed that she should rent the premises at a low price for the first year.
At that time, nobody in her family expected her to become a professional cook.
Her tiny kitchen at home was suddenly too small for so many orders.
Critics praise the simple dishes, which are made almost entirely from vegetables that would otherwise have been thrown away.
He tasted a bowl of her pumpkin soup and could not stop talking about it.
The kitchen was noisy and stressful, but every day brought a new lesson.

groups.instruction: Przeczytaj teksty, w których pięć osób (A–E) opowiada o swoich porannych nawykach. Dla każdego pytania (1–15) wybierz osobę A–E. Każda osoba może być wybrana więcej niż jeden raz.
groups.text:
Five people describe the habits that start their day. (Persons A–E)

A – Priya, software developer
I get up at five, long before the rest of the family, and write a novel in the kitchen for an hour. Nobody at my office knows about it. My first book was turned down by several publishers, which hurt more than I admit, but I decided to try again. I never drink coffee in the morning – the writing wakes me up better than any caffeine.

B – Marek, taxi driver
Every morning I swim in the lake, even in winter. I began after a back injury, when the doctor advised gentle exercise, and I was the first to laugh at the idea. Then a friend dared me to try cold water just once. I have not missed a day since, and my doctor still cannot believe how much better I feel.

C – Hannah, teacher
Five minutes of silence at the start of each lesson were not my idea. I read about it in a magazine and was very doubtful, because my students rarely stay quiet for five seconds. To my surprise they enjoyed it, and when I once forgot, they reminded me. Now we do it every day, and it helps especially before exams.

D – Carlos, baker
My day begins at two in the morning, so I am in bed by six in the evening. That means I miss most family dinners, which I really regret. But I love the empty streets and the silence of the city, and I often watch the sun rise from the roof of the bakery. My wife brings me lunch at noon, which makes the long day easier.

E – Julia, student
Before my first lecture I walk dogs at the animal shelter. I cannot keep a pet in my room, and this is the best way to spend time with animals. I want to become a vet one day, and the shelter staff let me watch how they treat the sick animals. Getting up so early was difficult at first, but I do not mind it now.

(Tekst został wymyślony na potrzeby ćwiczenia.)
